title: Physiological and performance responses to a 6-day taper in middle-distance runners: influence of training frequency
authors: Mujika I, Goya A, Ruiz E, Grijalba A, Santisteban J, Padilla S
population: Male middle-distance runners after 18 weeks of training
findings: 9 male middle-distance runners were assigned to a high frequency taper (training daily, n=5) or a moderate frequency taper (resting every third day, n=4); taper was an 80% nonlinear progressive reduction in high intensity interval training.
800 m performance improved significantly after the high frequency taper (121.8 +/- 4.7 vs 124.2 +/- 4.9 s, p < 0.05) but not after the moderate frequency taper (126.6 +/- 2.8 vs 127.1 +/- 2.1 s).
Peak blood lactate and total testosterone increased with taper; the change in peak lactate correlated with change in serum cortisol (r = -0.75) and testosterone:cortisol ratio (r = 0.82).
Authors conclude that training daily during a 6-day taper brought significant performance gains, whereas resting every third day did not.
limitations: Very small parallel groups (5 vs 4), 800 m runners (not distance or marathon), 6-day taper; the 'crossover' design label was wrong, it was a two-group comparison.
implications: Keep scheduled run days in the final taper week (short easy runs, shorter quality) rather than adding rest days; any frequency cut should stay within about 20% (Mujika & Padilla).
Extrapolation to ultras and marathons is untested; treat as a default, not a hard rule.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (IJSM Jul 2002). Design changed from experimental-crossover to other (parallel groups, assignment method unstated).
